objectives: Convert between Snellen and LogMAR notations and explain why LogMAR is the research standard.
Describe the workflow of objective and subjective refraction: retinoscopy, autorefraction, the phoropter, and the Jackson cross-cylinder.
Read and interpret a spectacle prescription specified by sphere, cylinder, axis, and add.

slides.title: Measuring acuity — Snellen, the minute of arc, and LogMAR
slides.body:
**Visual acuity** is the eye's ability to resolve fine spatial detail, and it is the single most reported number in optometry. Its modern definition rests on the **minimum angle of resolution (MAR)** — the smallest angular separation, in **minutes of arc** (1 arcmin $= 1/60^\circ$), at which two features can be distinguished. Normal acuity corresponds to resolving detail subtending **1 arcmin**, an observation systematised by **Herman Snellen** (1834–1908) in **1862**.

The **Snellen chart** presents rows of letters (**optotypes**) of decreasing size, each constructed so that at the testing distance its critical detail (e.g. the gap in a letter) subtends a defined angle. **Snellen notation** is a fraction: $\tfrac{\text{test distance}}{\text{distance at which the letter subtends } 5\,\text{arcmin}}$. Thus **20/20** (or **6/6** in metres) means the patient reads at 20 feet what a standard eye reads at 20 feet; **20/40** means they must be at 20 feet to read what a normal eye reads at 40. The whole optotype subtends **5 arcmin** and each stroke **1 arcmin** at the 'denominator' distance.

Snellen charts have flaws an examiner must respect: unequal numbers of letters per line, irregular size steps, and crowding that varies down the chart. These were fixed by the **LogMAR chart**, developed by **Ian Bailey** and **Jan Lovie** in **1976** and adopted by the **Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS)**. The ETDRS chart has **five equally legible letters per line**, equal spacing, and a **constant 0.1 log-unit size progression**. **LogMAR** is the base-10 logarithm of the MAR in arcmin:
$$\text{LogMAR} = \log_{10}(\text{MAR})$$
so $\text{MAR} = 1\,\text{arcmin}$ gives $\text{LogMAR} = 0.00$ (i.e. 20/20), $\text{MAR} = 2$ gives $\text{LogMAR} = 0.30$ (20/40), and supernormal vision gives **negative** LogMAR (20/16 is about $-0.10$). Because each letter is worth $0.02$ logMAR and lines are evenly spaced, LogMAR allows **letter-by-letter scoring** and proper statistics, which is why it is the standard in clinical trials.

The relationship between the notations is exact: $\text{LogMAR} = \log_{10}\!\left(\tfrac{\text{denominator}}{\text{numerator}}\right)$. So a Snellen value of 20/63 is $\log_{10}(63/20) = \log_{10}(3.15) \approx 0.50$ logMAR. The **decimal acuity** notation (used in much of Europe) is simply the Snellen fraction evaluated, e.g. 20/40 = 0.5. **Edmund Landolt**'s **broken-ring** optotype (the **Landolt C**, 1888) and the **tumbling E** offer language-independent alternatives used worldwide and in children.

slides.title: Objective refraction — retinoscopy and autorefraction
slides.body:
Before asking the patient anything, the optometrist can measure the refractive error **objectively** — without the patient's judgement. This is essential in infants, in patients who cannot communicate, and as a fast, reliable starting point for everyone.

**Retinoscopy** is the classic objective technique, traceable to **Ferdinand Cuignet** (1873) and refined by many. The examiner shines a streak or spot of light into the eye and observes the **reflex** moving across the pupil as the light is swept. By neutralising the movement of the reflex with **trial lenses** (or the retinoscopy rack), the examiner finds the lens power that makes the reflex fill the pupil all at once — the **point of neutrality**. The principle is **conjugacy**: at neutrality, the patient's retina is conjugate with the examiner's peephole. Because the examiner works at arm's length, a **working-distance correction** is subtracted: at $66\,\text{cm}$ the correction is $1/0.66 \approx +1.50\,\text{D}$. A reflex that moves **with** the streak ('with' movement) indicates the far point is behind the examiner (add plus); 'against' movement indicates plus over-correction (add minus). Retinoscopy uniquely detects **astigmatism**, because the reflex shows a brighter, oriented streak along the principal meridians.

**Autorefraction** automates the objective measurement with an instrument that projects an infrared target into the eye and analyses the returning wavefront or image sharpness, typically using a **Scheiner-style** double-pinhole, image-analysis, or **Hartmann–Shack wavefront** sensor (after **Johannes Hartmann** and **Roland Shack**). The autorefractor outputs an estimate of **sphere, cylinder, and axis** in seconds. Its main pitfall is **instrument myopia / proximal accommodation**: the patient may over-accommodate on the near-feeling internal target, biasing the result toward minus, so the device uses fogging and a 'fixation-at-infinity' picture, and the result is always confirmed subjectively.

Both methods deliver a **starting prescription** that the optometrist then refines. In children and strong latent hyperopes, accommodation must be paralysed first with **cycloplegic** drops (**cyclopentolate**, **atropine**, or **tropicamide**) so the relaxed refractive state is revealed — **cycloplegic retinoscopy** is the reference standard in paediatric refraction. The objective result also serves as a safety check: a large discrepancy between objective and subjective findings flags possible **keratoconus**, media opacity, or a non-organic component. In short, objective refraction tells the clinician roughly where the answer lies; the next step pins it down with the patient's own judgement.

slides.title: Subjective refraction, the cross-cylinder, and reading a prescription
slides.body:
**Subjective refraction** refines the objective starting point using the patient's reported preference, almost always behind a **phoropter** (also called a **refractor head**) — the familiar instrument containing stacked spherical and cylindrical lenses, rotary prisms, and the **Jackson cross-cylinder**. The classic sequence is: best-sphere by **maximum plus to maximum visual acuity** (fogging then reducing plus, or the **duochrome / red–green** test in which the patient balances clarity of letters on red versus green backgrounds, exploiting the eye's longitudinal chromatic aberration), then cylinder, then a binocular balance.

The **Jackson cross-cylinder (JCC)**, attributed to **Edward Jackson** (1856–1942), is a lens with equal-magnitude plus and minus cylinders at right angles (e.g. $\pm 0.25\,\text{D}$) mounted so it can be flipped about its handle. It refines astigmatism in two stages. First the **axis** is checked: the JCC is straddled across the trial cylinder's axis and flipped; the patient reports which side is clearer, and the axis is rotated toward the clearer position until both flips look equal. Then the **power** is checked: the JCC axes are aligned with the cylinder axis and flipped; cylinder power is added or subtracted until the two flips are equal. The endpoint for both is **equality** of the two presentations.

The result is written as a **spectacle prescription** with up to four parts per eye:
- **Sphere (DS)** — the spherical power in diopters (plus for hyperopia, minus for myopia).
- **Cylinder (DC)** — the additional power in one meridian to correct astigmatism.
- **Axis** — the orientation (in degrees, $1$–$180$, using the **TABO** convention) of the cylinder; specifically the axis is **perpendicular** to the meridian of greatest cylindrical power in minus-cyl notation.
- **Add** — the extra plus power for near work in presbyopes, the same for both eyes.

A typical entry reads: **OD $-2.50$ / $-1.00 \times 180$, Add $+2.00$** (right eye, $-2.50\,\text{D}$ sphere, $-1.00\,\text{D}$ cylinder at axis $180^\circ$, with a $+2.00\,\text{D}$ near add); **OS** denotes the left eye and **OU** both. The **spherical equivalent** — useful for contact lenses and quick comparison — is $\text{SE} = \text{sphere} + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{cylinder}$, so this eye's SE is $-2.50 + \tfrac{1}{2}(-1.00) = -3.00\,\text{D}$. Notation can be transposed between **plus-cyl** and **minus-cyl** form by: (1) adding the cylinder to the sphere, (2) flipping the cylinder sign, and (3) rotating the axis by $90^\circ$. Mastering this 'sphere/cylinder/axis/add' grammar — and the SE shortcut — is what lets an optometrist communicate a refraction unambiguously to a dispensing optician or a contact-lens lab.

question.question: A patient's acuity is recorded as Snellen 20/40. Convert this to LogMAR using $\text{LogMAR} = \log_{10}(\text{denominator}/\text{numerator})$. Give the answer to two decimal places.
Why is the ETDRS/LogMAR chart preferred over the traditional Snellen chart in clinical research?
options: It uses larger letters so that more patients can read it.
It has an equal number of equally legible letters per line, equal spacing, and a constant 0.1 log-unit size progression, enabling letter-by-letter scoring and valid statistics.
It eliminates the need to specify a testing distance.
It measures colour vision in addition to acuity.
question.explanation: The Bailey–Lovie/ETDRS LogMAR design fixes the statistical defects of the Snellen chart: every line has the same number of letters (five), the letters are matched for legibility, spacing is proportional and uniform, and size changes in equal 0.1 log-unit steps. This lets each letter contribute 0.02 logMAR, so acuity can be scored letter-by-letter and analysed with parametric statistics — essential for trials. It is not about larger letters (A), it still requires a defined test distance (C), and it does not assess colour (D).

hints: Think about what makes a measurement statistically valid and repeatable.
Count the letters per line and the size steps.
slides.workedSolution: The LogMAR (Bailey–Lovie 1976 / ETDRS) chart standardises everything that varies on a Snellen chart: five equally legible letters per row, uniform proportional spacing, and a constant 0.1 log-unit progression in size. This permits letter-by-letter scoring (0.02 logMAR each) and proper statistical analysis, which is exactly why it is the research standard. Option B is correct.

question.question: A prescription reads sphere $-1.50\,\text{D}$ with cylinder $-2.00\,\text{D}$. Compute the spherical equivalent, $\text{SE} = \text{sphere} + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{cylinder}$, in diopters with its sign.
During subjective refraction the Jackson cross-cylinder is used in two stages. Which describes the correct endpoints?
options: Both axis and power are set by finding the lens that gives the single brightest reflex.
Axis is refined by rotating toward the flip the patient prefers until both flips look equal; power is refined by adding/subtracting cylinder until both flips look equal.
Axis is found by neutralising the retinoscopy reflex; power is found with the duochrome test.
The cross-cylinder sets only the sphere, never the cylinder.
question.explanation: The Jackson cross-cylinder (Edward Jackson) refines astigmatism by seeking equality, not a single best image. For axis: straddle the trial-cylinder axis with the JCC, flip, and rotate the cylinder axis toward whichever flip the patient prefers, repeating until the two flips appear equal. For power: align the JCC axes with the cylinder axis, flip, and increase or decrease cylinder power until the two presentations are equally clear (equally blurred). The 'brightest reflex' (option A) describes retinoscopy, the duochrome (option C) refines the sphere not the cylinder axis, and the JCC absolutely does set cylinder, not just sphere (option D).

hints: The cross-cylinder works by making two flipped views look the same.
First the axis, then the power, each ending in 'equality'.
slides.workedSolution: The JCC is flipped between two states and the patient chooses the clearer; you adjust until neither is preferred. Axis refinement rotates the cylinder toward the favoured flip until equality; power refinement (JCC axes aligned with the cylinder axis) adds or removes cylinder until equality. Both endpoints are 'the two flips look the same.' That is option B.

question.question: Interpreting a written prescription for a presbyopic astigmat
question.prompt: A dispensing optician hands you a card reading: 'OD $-3.00$ / $-1.50 \times 175$, OS $-2.75$ / $-1.00 \times 010$, Add $+2.25$.' Explain in plain terms what each component (sphere, cylinder, axis, add) means for each eye, compute the spherical equivalent of the right eye, and explain what the single Add value will be used for and why it is the same for both eyes. Finally, state what kind of refractive errors this patient has and roughly what lens type (single-vision, bifocal, or progressive) might suit them.
